How Patients Choose a Doctor Online: Search, Maps, Reviews and AI Answers

Nov 2, 2026The SocialDM Insights Team6 min read
Key takeaways
  • Patients usually search, compare practices on the map, read reviews and check your website before they call.
  • Google says local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and more reviews and positive ratings can help.
  • A June 2026 KFF poll found 29% of U.S. adults use AI tools for health information at least monthly, up from 17% in 2024.
  • Clear service and provider pages, a current insurance list and hours that match your Google profile help patients choose you.
In this article
  1. Where do patients start looking for a practice?
  2. How does Google decide which practices appear on the map?
  3. How much do reviews matter when patients choose a practice?
  4. Are patients using AI tools to find health information and providers?
  5. What do patients check on your website before they book?
  6. What should a practice fix first?

Most patients now choose a practice in a few quick steps: they search Google or ask an AI tool, compare the practices that appear on the map, read reviews, and then check a website to confirm the practice takes their insurance and can see them soon. If your practice is missing, wrong or vague at any of those steps, you can lose the patient before your front desk ever knows they were looking.

None of this replaces referrals. Even a referred patient will usually search your name, and what they find decides whether they call.

Where do patients start looking for a practice?

Most start with a search that pairs a need with a place, such as a specialty, a service or a symptom plus their town, on Google Search or Google Maps. Others start with a name from a referral and search that name to check the practice before calling.

Those two starting points need different things from you. The referred patient already knows your name, so your job is to confirm the referral was a good one: accurate hours, a working phone number, recent reviews and a clear way to book. The patient searching by need does not know you exist yet, so you have to be relevant and visible for the services you actually want to grow. When we audit a practice, the gap is almost always on the second side. A practice can rank first for its own name and barely appear for the services it most wants to sell.

How does Google decide which practices appear on the map?

Google says local results are based mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. Relevance is how well your profile matches the search, distance is how far you are from the person searching, and prominence is how well known you are, including how many reviews you have.

That comes from Google's own page on how to improve local ranking, which also says complete and accurate business information helps match you to the right searches, that more reviews and positive ratings can help, and that there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. You cannot move your office closer to every patient, so the work goes into relevance and prominence: a complete, correct profile, the right categories, real photos, steady reviews and a website that backs up what the profile says.

How much do reviews matter when patients choose a practice?

Reviews do two jobs at once. Google counts them toward prominence, and patients read them to judge whether your practice is organized, respectful and easy to deal with. A patient comparing three practices on the map can decide on reviews alone.

Your replies are public too. A reply that is calm and general reassures the next patient. A defensive reply, or one that mentions details of someone's visit, does real damage, and in healthcare it can also create a privacy problem. Before anyone on your team replies to a review, make sure they know never to confirm that the reviewer is a patient or say anything about their care.

Are patients using AI tools to find health information and providers?

A growing share are. A KFF poll published in June 2026 found that 29% of U.S. adults use AI tools or chatbots for health information or advice at least monthly, up from 17% in 2024. That measures health information in general, not choosing a doctor, so treat it as a sign of habit rather than a booking figure.

The practical point is that AI answers draw on what they can read. Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in its AI features, which means ordinary SEO basics still apply. Other assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity may describe your practice using your website, your Google profile, directories and review sites. If your insurance list lives in a PDF, your provider bios are thin, or two directories show different hours, an AI answer can repeat the wrong version. I would not promise any practice a place in AI answers. I would make sure the facts those tools find are correct and easy to read.

What do patients check on your website before they book?

They check whether you can help them, whether you take their insurance, who they will see, where you are, when you are open and how to book. If any of those take more than a few seconds to find, it is easy for a patient to go back to the map and pick the next practice.

What the patient wants to knowWhat the page should show
Can you help with my problem?A page for each main service or condition you treat, written in plain language and approved by a clinician
Do you take my insurance?A current list of accepted plans on a normal web page, with a date it was last checked
Who will I see?A page for each provider with credentials, specialties, languages spoken and locations
Are you taking new patients?A clear yes or no, by provider if it differs
Where and when?Address, parking or access notes and hours that match your Google profile exactly
How do I book?One obvious phone number and, if you offer it, an online booking link that works on a phone

Service and provider pages do most of the work here, for patients and for search engines. A single "Services" page with a bulleted list gives Google and AI tools very little to match against a specific search.

What should a practice fix first?

Start with accuracy, then coverage. Make sure every location's Google profile, website and major directories agree on name, address, phone number, hours and providers, and then build out the service and provider pages patients need to choose you.

  1. Search like a patient. From a phone, search your top three services plus your town, on Google, on Maps and in one AI tool.
  2. Fix your Google Business Profile. Check hours, holiday hours, categories, phone number, booking link and photos at every location.
  3. Check provider listings. Make sure departed providers are not still listed as seeing patients, and that current ones appear correctly.
  4. Set up a steady review routine. Ask every patient the same way, with no incentives, and reply in general terms.
  5. Publish the missing pages. One page per main service and one per provider, with insurance and booking information easy to find.

Questions we hear

How do most patients find a new doctor today?

Many search Google or Google Maps for a service or specialty plus their town, compare the practices that appear, read reviews and then check the website. Referred patients usually search the practice name before calling.

Do online reviews affect where a practice shows up on Google Maps?

Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking, as part of prominence. Reviews also matter because patients read them, and the replies, before choosing.

Are patients using ChatGPT or other AI tools to choose a doctor?

Some are using AI tools for health information. A June 2026 KFF poll found 29% of U.S. adults do so at least monthly, though that figure covers health information broadly, not choosing a provider.

What should be on a medical practice website for patients to book?

Clear pages for each main service and provider, a current insurance list, whether you are accepting new patients, hours that match your Google profile and one simple way to book.

Can a practice pay Google for a better Maps ranking?

No. Google says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. Ads are a separate product.
